To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) oxidative stress may drive aberrant translation in Alzheimer’s disease (b) the cell survival response may inadvertently up-regulates the translation of proteins implicated with Alzheimer’s disease.

aberrant translation of BACE1 may be driven by the presence of an upstream open reading framework within the BACE5 5’ UTR and that the translation of BACE5 may be enhanced in the presence of oxidative stress, a condition which is known to occur in AD.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the translation of proteins linked with AD.
the regulation of protein synthesis at the point of mRNA translation.
the translation of proteins implicated with Alzheimer’s disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
aberrant translation is a key step in the regulation and manufacture of proteins implicated in the pathology of AD.
the translation of proteins linked to Alzheimer’s disease may be enhanced or repressed by several mechanisms.

the translational efficiency is a key regulator of the production of amyloid precursor proteins, the amyloid precursor protein cleavage enzymes, and the downstream amyloid beta peptides implicated in the pathology of Alzheimer’s disease (Figure 1).
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have demonstrated that the translation machinery can be manipulated to increase the levels of a protein that is protective against the pathology of Alzheimer’s disease, while at the same time decreasing the levels of a secretase responsible for generating the Abeta42 peptide, a protein that has been linked with the pathology.

we have identified that the cell stress response can enhance the translation of proteins implicated as causative factors in Alzheimer’s disease, and that these stressors may enhance the translation efficiency of these proteins via the activation of a uORF located within the mRNA of the protein of interest.

we identified a novel mechanism for the regulation of BACE1 expression, a protein which is responsible for the cleavage of the amyloid precursor protein (APP) into the amyloid beta peptide (Abeta), a peptide which is implicated in the pathology of AD.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we have demonstrated that the translation of BACE1, an AD-associated protein, can be regulated at the point of initiation by a uORF located within the 5’ UTR of the BACE1 mRNA.
the translation initiation machinery is a key regulatory step in the synthesis of proteins associated with the pathology of AD.
the cell survival pathway may inadvertently drive the translation of proteins implicated with AD pathology.
